title: Ukraine's Mood Swing
gist: New SOCIS polling shows Ukrainians now rank corruption above the war itself as their top concern and would vote Zelensky out by roughly 2-to-1 against any of three rivals (Zaluzhny, Fedorov, Budanov), driven by a cascade of corruption scandals inside his tightly centralized inner circle and his office's pushback against anti-corruption investigators — a political fragility risk with direct implications for wartime governance, aid conditionality, and eventual postwar elections.

insights.claim: SOCIS polling from early August shows 90 percent of Ukrainians believe corruption is at a high or extremely high level, and nearly 57 percent blame Zelensky for it — nearly double the share who blamed him in a comparable SOCIS poll from April 2025.
insights.speaker: Adrian Karatnycky
insights.so_what: A near-doubling in a single year of the share of Ukrainians personally blaming Zelensky for corruption is a leading indicator of leadership-transition risk that could affect ceasefire negotiation dynamics and postwar governance stability.
insights.locator: Recent polling from Ukrainian political research company SOCIS

insights.claim: SOCIS polling projects that in a hypothetical second-round election, Zelensky would lose decisively to any of three rivals: former commander in chief Valery Zaluzhny (34% to 66%), former defense minister Mykhaylo Fedorov (36% to 64%), or intelligence chief Kyrylo Budanov (38% to 62%).
insights.speaker: Adrian Karatnycky
insights.so_what: A roughly 2-to-1 hypothetical loss margin against three separate rivals indicates the erosion is broad and not tied to any single opposition figure — a structural, not personality-driven, decline in Zelensky's mandate.
insights.locator: the SOCIS polling indicates that in a second round

insights.claim: 55 percent of Ukrainians believe Zelensky is governing ineffectively, yet the public still shows unity in supporting him as wartime commander in chief even while rejecting his domestic policies and governing style; Zelensky retains a loyalist core of just over 20 percent of voters.
insights.speaker: Adrian Karatnycky
insights.so_what: The split between wartime-commander support and domestic-governance disapproval suggests Zelensky's authority is contingent on the war continuing — a peace deal or ceasefire could rapidly convert into a political crisis for him.

insights.claim: Almost two-thirds of Ukrainians surveyed say elections should be held quickly in the event of a negotiated ceasefire or peace deal, even though Ukraine's constitution currently bars elections during wartime.
insights.speaker: Adrian Karatnycky
insights.so_what: Any ceasefire negotiation should be read as also triggering a near-term Ukrainian election cycle with high odds of a leadership change — relevant for assessing continuity risk in Ukraine's negotiating posture, reconstruction contracts, and reform commitments post-ceasefire.

themes.theme: Corruption scandals inside Zelensky's inner circle

insights.claim: Four of Zelensky's top managers have been implicated in corruption: former deputy presidential-office head Andriy Smyrnov was indicted for illicit enrichment and money laundering; former economic-affairs deputy head Rostyslav Shurma was served notice of suspicion over a scheme involving his brother's solar-power 'green tariffs' and now lives in Germany; deputy office head Oleh Tatarov's bribery case was transferred from the independent NABU to the loyalist-controlled prosecutor general's office; and former chief of staff Andriy Yermak was charged with money laundering tied to luxury housing and is free on bail.
insights.speaker: Adrian Karatnycky
insights.so_what: A cluster of simultaneous corruption cases against Zelensky's closest deputies indicates systemic (not isolated) graft risk in Ukraine's wartime procurement and energy-subsidy administration — relevant for reconstruction-fund governance and donor conditionality design.
insights.locator: Andriy Smyrnov, a former deputy head of the presidential office

insights.claim: Deputy presidential-office head Iryna Mudra was dismissed in August amid a NABU investigation ('Operation Forrest Gump') into an alleged $3.3 million money-laundering scheme conducted through a state-owned bank to fund bail for a former government minister; wiretapped calls suggest she acted on the instruction of a 'chief,' widely believed by Ukrainian journalists to be presidential-office head Kyrylo Budanov, acting at Zelensky's behest.
insights.speaker: Adrian Karatnycky
insights.so_what: Wiretap evidence implicating a chain of command reaching toward Zelensky himself (via Budanov) raises the stakes of the scandal beyond individual bad actors to the presidency's own conduct.
insights.locator: On Aug. 19, Iryna Mudra was dismissed

insights.claim: A major scandal involves Timur Mindich, Zelensky's business partner in his film/TV production company, allegedly part of a criminal group including a former justice minister, a former energy minister, a former deputy prime minister, and Zelensky's own chief of staff, engaged in extortion and profiting from state institution revenue; wiretaps also suggest Rustem Umerov — just named to run Ukraine's foreign intelligence service — may have worked to advance Mindich's private business interests.
insights.speaker: Adrian Karatnycky
insights.so_what: A named associate of the newly appointed foreign-intelligence chief allegedly tied to a corruption ring is a material governance red flag for any Western intelligence-sharing or aid arrangement involving that agency.
insights.locator: a major corruption scandal involves Timur Mindich

themes.theme: Governance by a small centralized circle

insights.claim: Zelensky declared in December 2023 that he relies on a team of just five to six key managers to run the country's affairs — a highly centralized system of governance that, while in violation of the Ukrainian constitution, was long tolerated by the public as a wartime necessity.
insights.speaker: Adrian Karatnycky
insights.so_what: An extremely narrow decision-making circle concentrates both execution speed and corruption/single-point-of-failure risk — a structural governance factor relevant to any counterparty assessing Ukrainian state contract or aid-disbursement integrity.

insights.claim: Under Zelensky's presidency there have been eight ministers of defense and seven economic ministers, with each dismissal of a high-trust official — Gen. Valery Zaluzhny (Feb. 2024), foreign minister Dmytro Kuleba, and defense minister Mykhaylo Fedorov (after just six months, in mid-July) — eroding his public support.
insights.speaker: Adrian Karatnycky
insights.so_what: Extreme cabinet turnover (8 defense ministers, 7 economic ministers) signals policy discontinuity risk for any long-horizon defense-industrial or reconstruction partnership with the Ukrainian state.
insights.locator: Under his presidency, there have been eight ministers of defense

insights.claim: As the Mindich scandal emerged, Zelensky's administration used the prosecutor general and Ukrainian Security Service to open more than a dozen investigations into NABU agents and arrest several — including detective Viktor Husarov and top anti-corruption official Ruslan Mahamedrasulov, both investigating Zelensky's inner circle — on treason and enemy-trading charges, coupled with legislation to strip NABU and SAPO of independence; after mass protests and Western donor pressure, Zelensky reversed course and the charges against Husarov were dropped.
insights.speaker: Adrian Karatnycky
insights.so_what: A direct attempt to neuter independent anti-corruption institutions, reversed only under Western donor pressure, is a governance red flag Western aid conditionality frameworks should explicitly track going forward.
insights.locator: Zelensky's administration appears to have used the country's prosecutor general

themes.theme: Second-order risks to the war effort

insights.claim: The author warns that disaffection with Zelensky's leadership can affect battlefield morale and could worsen Ukraine's existing problem with draft evasion, at a moment when scarce anti-missile interceptors mean Russia is expected to seriously degrade Ukraine's electricity and heating this winter.
insights.speaker: Adrian Karatnycky
insights.so_what: Political corruption fatigue and infrastructure-attack risk are converging this winter — a compounding civil-resilience risk relevant to forecasting Ukrainian wartime economic stability and energy-infrastructure investment risk.
insights.locator: Zelensky's high levels of public disapproval carry risks.

insights.claim: Ukrainian civil society and grassroots activists — notably a small group of mainly women NGO activists who trained thousands of combatants in drone operations, initially funded via crowdfunding before the state took over — have been a major independent factor in the battlefield turnaround, separate from Zelensky's own leadership.
insights.speaker: Adrian Karatnycky
insights.so_what: Ukraine's drone-warfare capability has grassroots/crowdfunded origins rather than top-down state planning — relevant context for understanding the resilience of Ukraine's drone-industrial base independent of any political turnover at the top.
insights.locator: it was a small group of mainly women activists

insights.claim: The author's proposed fix is for Zelensky to reduce presidential centralization, form a government of national unity, and bring in untainted officials from rival parties and previously dismissed competent officials — but concludes there is little indication Zelensky, who has always had absolute confidence in his own judgment, will take this step.
insights.speaker: Adrian Karatnycky
insights.so_what: The author's low-conviction prediction that Zelensky will not reform governance implies the corruption/legitimacy overhang is likely to persist through any near-term ceasefire negotiation rather than being resolved proactively.
insights.locator: Unfortunately, nothing suggests that Zelensky can take such a step.
